solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Incompatible staff given role following appeal

indicators.note: following says the role comes straight after the appeal in the line of letters

parts.note: a pole is a long staff
SA is short for sex appeal
an actor's role is a part

explanation.surface: A mismatched team member is handed a job after an appeal for help.
explanation.walkthrough: SA for sex appeal is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that are poles apart differ completely, like opposite ends of the globe, so they cannot be reconciled.

clue.text: Hard drink turned up in market

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: A strong drink is knocked back at a market stall.
explanation.walkthrough: H and SUP together read upwards give PUSH.
explanation.definitionFit: To push a product is to promote and sell it hard, which is what marketing does.

clue.text: Colourful bird from which bank of Liffey?

indicators.note: a river has a bank on each side, so a bank of a river's name is its first or last letter

parts.note: the left-hand bank of the word
asking which of two banks invites the answer 'this or that'
the right-hand bank of the word

explanation.surface: A bright bird is spotted by the Liffey, the river through Dublin, and we wonder which side it is on.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer to the question 'which bank of Liffey?' is 'L or Y', which spells the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A lory is a brightly plumaged parrot of Australasia, so it qualifies as a colourful bird.

clue.text: Reason clock stops working in American's holidays

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the mainspring of a clockwork mechanism snapping
second meaning: the US term for the vacation from college in March or April

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a little cryptic: when a clock's coil fails, it stops.
explanation.definitionFit: In the US, students take a week of vacation each spring, often travelling somewhere warm to party.

clue.text: Silly sports coats and old hat

indicators.note: to coat something is to wrap it on the outside, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: PE is physical education, school sports
a silly person is an ass

explanation.surface: Somebody's sports jackets and dated hat look ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly' looks like an adjective for the coats, but it is a noun-like fool and 'coats' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Old hat is an idiom for something out of fashion, the same as the borrowed French word for faded.

clue.text: Brought up-to-date wine plugged by European tax-free?

indicators.note: something plugged has a stopper pushed inside it, so other letters go within

parts.note: red is a kind of wine
E is the abbreviation for European
free of tax means no VAT, the British sales tax

explanation.surface: A modernised wine is sold without duty somewhere in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is value added tax, the UK's sales tax.
explanation.definitionFit: A renovated building has been restored and modernised, so it has been made current again.

clue.text: Saccharin oddly dropped as energy drink ingredient

indicators.note: losing the letters in odd positions leaves only the even-placed ones

parts.note: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A sweetener is left out of a sports drink recipe.
explanation.definitionFit: The berry of a South American palm is marketed as a superfood and blended into health and energy drinks.

clue.text: State commercial breaks Italy broadcast cease to work

parts.note: Cal is short for California, a US state

indicators.note: breaks means splits open, so the advert sits inside the other letters
broadcast means scattered, so the country's letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
an ad is a commercial

explanation.surface: A TV advert interrupts coverage of Italy and the broadcaster stops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' wants to be the definition (to say), but here it is the US state.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to stop working for the time being, as at the end of a working day.

clue.text: Ask to box good fighter, turning up to prevent cheating

definitions.note: describes the purpose of the verb rather than naming it

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so one set of letters goes inside the other

parts.note: to invite is to ask
G is the abbreviation for good

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Muhammad Ali, the boxer

explanation.surface: A boxing promoter asks a decent fighter to appear, hoping to stop a fixed bout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' and 'fighter' make it a boxing story; ALI read upwards is ILA.
explanation.definitionFit: Invigilators supervise students sitting an exam, and their job is to stop copying and crib notes.

clue.text: Leader of Soviet revolt stifles resistance, causing shock

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter

indicators.note: to stifle is to smother, so one letter is held inside the other word

parts.note: an uprising is a revolt
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A Soviet leader crushes a rebellion, to the world's dismay.
explanation.definitionFit: Something surprising is unexpected and so gives people a jolt of astonishment.

clue.text: Maybe Russian in bar almost drinking litre

indicators.note: drinking means taking in, so the shortened word swallows the other letter
almost means not quite all, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: bar and save both mean except, as in 'all bar one'
L is the abbreviation for litre

explanation.surface: A Russian, perhaps, sits in a bar nearly finishing a litre of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub, but it means except.
explanation.definitionFit: Russians are one of the Slavic peoples of eastern Europe, so a Russian is an example.

clue.text: In France, noble ruler's excessively liberal means of punishment

parts.note: duc is French for duke
a king is a ruler, with the possessive S
too means excessively
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A French aristocrat's overly lax monarch devises a way to punish people.
explanation.definitionFit: A chair on a long beam was used to plunge offenders, often scolds, into a pond as a public penalty.

clue.text: Seeking Parisian in Angola's capital gobbling sandwiches

parts.note: en is French for in

indicators.note: to sandwich something is to put it between layers, so one letter sits inside

parts.note: gobbling food is devouring it

indicators.note: a capital is a head letter, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: first letter of the country's name

explanation.surface: A Parisian in Luanda wolfs down sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' looks like food being gobbled, but it is the verb: DEVOURING holds the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Endeavouring and seeking both mean trying or attempting to achieve something, as in 'seeking to please'.

clue.text: Rich person in Ithaca developed test for believers

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the rearranged letters
developed means grown into a new form, so the place name's letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
a toff is a rich, upper-class person

explanation.surface: A wealthy man on the Greek island of Ithaca devises an exam for the faithful.
explanation.walkthrough: TOFF is British slang for a posh rich person.
explanation.definitionFit: An act of faith is something done trusting without proof, which tests and demonstrates a believer's conviction.

clue.text: Eastender's ashamed, inhabiting urban area in disrepair

indicators.note: to inhabit a place is to live inside it, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: a town is an urban area

indicators.note: a Cockney from London's East End traditionally drops the H sound at the start of words

parts.note: humbled means made to feel ashamed

explanation.surface: A shamefaced Londoner lives in a run-down part of the city.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys, from London's East End, are known for dropping the H at the start of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumbledown building is crumbling and falling apart, which is what being in disrepair means.

clue.text: Most stout and claret drained, with partners tucking in

indicators.note: tucking in means slotting inside, so one piece goes within the other
drained means emptied, so the inside letters go and only the outside pair stays

parts.note: first and last letters
hubbies are husbands, informal for partners

explanation.surface: Couples tuck into dinner, finishing the claret and the strongest stout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout' and 'claret' pretend to be drinks; stout is the adjective for plump.
explanation.definitionFit: Chubby means plump, as does stout, and the superlative form of each matches.

clue.text: Going out with no one, southern Frenchman's upset

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one
S is the abbreviation for southern
Serge is a common French man's name

explanation.surface: A Frenchman is unhappy at going out alone.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after Frenchman stands for 'is', joining the wordplay to the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Egression is the act of exiting or emerging, a formal noun for leaving a place.

clue.text: Two kings with large housing areas in African village

indicators.note: housing means giving shelter, so the outer letters hold the others inside

parts.note: K and R are both abbreviations for king, from chess and from Rex
L is the abbreviation for large
A is the abbreviation for area, and two areas give two of them

explanation.surface: A pair of monarchs with big residential zones live in an African village.
explanation.definitionFit: In southern Africa, a kraal is a traditional settlement of huts, often enclosed by a fence.

clue.text: Something played in prom breathtakingly

indicators.note: in says the answer sits within the following words

parts.note: spans the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A piece of music is performed brilliantly at the Proms concerts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Proms are a famous summer series of classical concerts in London, which makes 'played' sound musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Ombre is an old card game for three players, popular in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

clue.text: Useless and, for Marx, boring socialist worker, say

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so this word goes inside the others

parts.note: a red is a socialist
und is German for and, Marx being German
a worker is one kind of ant, so 'say' marks an example

explanation.surface: A dull Marxist labourer is judged useless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Socialist worker' looks like one political phrase, but it splits in two, and the German word goes between the halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Redundant means superfluous or no longer needed, so it is surplus to requirements.

clue.text: Dissolute rake seized by school head — odd character!

indicators.note: something seized is held in another's grip, so it sits within

parts.note: a school is a group of fish

indicators.note: dissolute means loose-living, so these letters are loosened into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A debauched libertine is grabbed by the headmaster, quite a strange fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School head' reads as headmaster, but the two words are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Freakishness means strangeness or abnormality, the quality of being odd in nature.

clue.text: Group's reason for not playing badminton?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a set of nine musicians
second meaning, read as two words: a court with nothing over the middle

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful split of the word into two.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is an ensemble of nine performers, and without a net strung across the court badminton cannot be played.

clue.text: What might swell looker sport as well as yuppie's jackets?

indicators.note: a jacket is the outside covering, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters
first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A dapper sporting yuppie wears a jacket meant to impress a beauty.
explanation.walkthrough: A looker is normally an attractive person; here it is the eye that looks.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the eyelid, and an eye is literally an organ that looks.

clue.text: Polish detective in film

indicators.note: in places the detective inside the film

parts.note: E.T. is the Spielberg film
DI is a Detective Inspector

explanation.surface: A detective from Poland appears in a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' wants to be the nationality, but it is the verb to refine.
explanation.definitionFit: To polish a text is to refine and improve its wording, which is editing.

clue.text: Humorous use of language, not unknown in press

indicators.note: not says the following item is taken away

parts.note: irony is saying the opposite of what is meant, for effect
Y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Wit and wordplay are kept out of the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' sounds like the newspapers, but it is the verb for smoothing clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To iron clothes is to press out the creases with a hot flat appliance.

clue.text: Showed the way job's secured in design originally

indicators.note: secured in means held fast inside, so one word goes within the other
originally means in an original, novel way, so the letters are made into something new

parts.note: taken as written
a post is a job; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: Someone shows the route because their job depends on it.
explanation.definitionFit: A signposted route has markers that direct travellers, so it has been pointed out for them.

clue.text: I'm grateful after unwrapping some yarn, say

indicators.note: once unwrapped, a word loses its outer covering, its first and last letters

parts.note: what you say when grateful

explanation.surface: Someone is thankful on opening a parcel of knitting wool.
explanation.definitionFit: A hank is a coil or measured length of wool or thread, so it is an example of a quantity of yarn.

clue.text: Left the setter twinkling rings, getting amount paid

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so the other letters go inside

parts.note: in a twinkling means in an instant
L is the abbreviation for left
the setter refers to themself as me

explanation.surface: The puzzle-maker leaves sparkling rings behind and receives a payment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rings' looks like jewellery, but it is the verb for surrounding.
explanation.definitionFit: An instalment is one of a series of part payments of a debt, so it is a sum handed over.
